notes.title: Chapter map: Functions, scope & closures
notes.html:
A function is an object made at runtime that can carry its surroundings with it. Each note adds one layer on top of the last. Read each arrow as a sentence: decorators built on closures.

Green = CORE, blue = SUPPORTING, grey = another chapter (dashed edges).

Reading order:09 LEGB10 closures11 arguments12 decorators13 functools
  • The one big idea: scope is decided at compile time (09), a closure takes the enclosing cells with it and reads them at call time (10), a decorator is just f = deco(f) with a closure as the wrapper (12), and functools gives the common wrappers a name and a lifetime (13). *args, **kwargs (11) is how a wrapper passes any call through.
  • The two most-confused pairs: late binding vs early binding: a closure reads its variable when called, so loop lambdas all see the last value, while a default argument is evaluated once at def time (10, and 03 in the data model) · lru_cache vs cached_property: a cache on the function that pins every self, vs a value stored on the instance (13, the picture).
  • Ten minutes before an interview: the TL;DR of 09 and 10, then 12's TL;DR (application bottom-up, execution top-down) and 13's picture.
  • Cross-chapter: names & binding (what a scope binds) · generators (a closure keeps variables, a generator keeps the whole call) · descriptors (property and cached_property are decorator-built descriptors).

No decision tree: these notes are layers, not alternatives.

notes.title: Scope & the LEGB Rule
notes.html:
References

Tutorial: scopes and namespaces · Execution model: naming and binding · The global statement · The nonlocal statement · Real Python: Scope and the LEGB rule

TL;DR

Reading searches outward: Local → Enclosing → Global → Built-in, first hit wins. Assigning declares: at compile time, for the whole function, retroactively.

Flow:compiler scans the bodyassigned anywhere: local (LOAD_FAST)captured from an outer function: cell (LOAD_DEREF)otherwise: LOAD_GLOBAL searches the module dict, then builtinsfirst hit wins

Recall

Prompt Answer
LEGB order? Local → Enclosing → Global → Built-in; the search stops at the first hit.
When is a name local? At compile time, if assigned anywhere in the body, even after the read.
UnboundLocalError vs NameError? Empty local slot (LOAD_FAST) vs missing from module and builtins (LOAD_GLOBAL).
global vs nonlocal? Compiler directives: rebind the module name vs the nearest enclosing function name.
What counts as assignment? =, +=, for targets, import, def, class, with/except … as, walrus.
Draw by hand: LEGB Nested boxes B ⊃ G ⊃ E ⊃ L; a read searches outward, first hit wins; a class body is off the path.

The idea

You use module-level names inside functions without declaring them, and it just works:

LIMIT = 10
def check(n): return n < LIMIT
check(3)                  # ① → True   L miss, E miss, G hit: stop

Reading searches four namespaces in order and stops at the first hit. That's also why def len(...) at module level breaks every len() call in that module: G is searched before B, so built-ins aren't privileged, just last. By default a name you only read is found by searching outward.

Now add one line after the read:

def check(n):
    result = n < LIMIT    # unchanged line...
    LIMIT = 99            # ...but this now exists
    return result
check(3)                  # ② → UnboundLocalError: cannot access local variable 'LIMIT'

The error is on the line you didn't edit. An assignment anywhere in the body makes the name local for the whole body, decided once by scanning the function before any of it runs. So the read never looks outward; it goes to an empty local slot and raises. global LIMIT (module) or nonlocal LIMIT (enclosing function) tells the compiler to route assignment outward instead.

The trade: Python gives you fast, statically-known locals and no declarations, and in exchange assignment silently acts as the declaration, for the whole function, retroactively.

How it works

The compiler classifies each name once; only the G and B dicts are ever searched at runtime:

The rules behind that classification (class-body and nonlocal rows verified on CPython 3.12):

Rule What actually happens
Classification is baked into the code object In CPython, locals go in co_varnames and compile to LOAD_FAST, a direct array index. Names shared with inner functions go in co_cellvars / co_freevars and compile to LOAD_DEREF: that's the E, a closure cell. Everything else compiles to LOAD_GLOBAL.
Two errors, two opcodes UnboundLocalError is LOAD_FAST on an empty slot: the name is known local, so there's no fallback. NameError is LOAD_GLOBAL missing in both dicts.
global and nonlocal don't execute They change which opcode the compiler emits, so nonlocal x with no enclosing binding is a compile-time SyntaxError, and nonlocal never reaches module scope.
Class bodies aren't an E Methods don't close over the class namespace, so a bare rate inside a method is a NameError (see the picture); go through self or the class.

Code

global for a single-writer singleton, nonlocal for state private to one closure:

_pool = None

def get_pool():
    global _pool                  # without it, the assignment makes _pool local
    if _pool is None:             # and this read raises UnboundLocalError
        _pool = create_pool()     # one writer, set once: the defensible use
    return _pool

def make_rate_limiter(limit: int):
    used = 0                      # a cell, private to each limiter
    def allow() -> bool:
        nonlocal used             # assigned below, so must be declared
        if used >= limit:         # only read: free variable, no declaration
            return False
        used += 1
        return True
    return allow

Break it: read the compiler's decision before calling anything.

x = "module-level"
def reads_only(): return x
def reads_then_assigns():
    y = x                         # identical line
    x = "local"
    return y
print(reads_only.__code__.co_varnames, reads_then_assigns.__code__.co_varnames)
print(reads_only()); reads_then_assigns()
# look for: 'x' in the second co_varnames before any call; only that one raises
# naive model predicts: both read the module x, since the assignment comes later

You get () ('y', 'x'), then module-level, then UnboundLocalError. Scope is a property of the compiled function, not execution order, and printing co_varnames is also the fastest way to debug a real one.

Interview

30-second answer: LEGB is the order Python searches for a name you read: Local, Enclosing function, Global module, then Built-ins, stopping at the first hit. The catch is that assignment anywhere in a function makes the name local for the entire body, decided at compile time. So reading it before the assignment raises UnboundLocalError instead of falling back to the global. global and nonlocal override that.

Q · Mechanism — Why does x += 1 fail inside a function when a global x exists? The compiler scans the whole body first. += is an assignment, so x goes into co_varnames and every reference compiles to LOAD_FAST. The read on the right-hand side hits an empty slot and raises. There's no fallback because the interpreter isn't searching; it already knows where x lives. That's why it's UnboundLocalError, not NameError. global x changes the emitted opcode.

Q · Failure — [lambda: i for i in range(3)] returns three handlers that all return 2. Why, and how do you fix it? Resolution is correct: each lambda finds the enclosing i. But closures capture the cell, not its value, and read it when called, by which point the loop left i == 2. Single-item tests pass, so it ships as retry callbacks all hitting the last URL. Fixes: lambda i=i: i (defaults are evaluated at def-time, so each snapshots), a factory make(i) creating a fresh cell per call, or functools.partial. The default form changes the public signature; the factory doesn't.

Q · Design — A config module mutates globals via global, and it went flaky under a new thread pool. Redesign the scope discipline. The binding constraint: global-mutated state is process-wide and unsynchronised, so racing workers get torn reads and lost updates. Build a frozen Config once at startup and pass it in, turning a hidden dependency into a parameter (and removing test monkeypatching). Per-request mutable state goes in a ContextVar: threading.local breaks under asyncio, where many tasks share a thread. global survives only for constants bound at import. First check: a concurrency test firing two requests with different config and asserting responses don't cross.

Compare

Read outer name Rebind outer name No binding exists
default LEGB search creates a local instead NameError at runtime
global x module scope rebinds module x created on assignment
nonlocal x nearest enclosing function rebinds that x SyntaxError at compile time

Pitfalls

  • "Python falls back to the global if the local isn't set yet"
    Never. The compiler fixes each name's scope for the whole function.
    ↳ Why: one assignment anywhere makes the name local everywhere in that function.
    ↳ Symptom: reading it first raises UnboundLocalError, not the global's value.
  • "Closures created in a loop capture the current value"
    They capture the variable's cell and read it when called.
    ↳ Symptom: the loop has finished, so every closure sees the last value.
    ↳ Fix: bind at creation: lambda i=i: i or functools.partial.
  • Not the same as late binding
    ↳ Difference: LEGB decides where a name is found; closures decide when it's read.
    ↳ So: the loop bug is timing, not lookup, which is why fixing scope doesn't fix it.
  • Don't use global to pass data between functions.
    ↳ Why: hidden coupling to call order, tests that depend on each other, and a data race under threads.
    ↳ Instead: pass arguments, return values.
  • Don't shadow built-ins (list, id, type, input, sum).
    ↳ Why: the assignment works; the TypeError appears later and far away, when list(...) hits your variable.
  • Don't grow a closure past two or three captured variables.
    ↳ Why: the state hides in __closure__ cells, out of sight of debuggers and tests.
    ↳ Instead: a small class with named attributes.
  • 🔖 Version: rules are stable across Python 3; comprehensions have had their own scope since 3.0 (late binding still applies inside).
    ↳ 3.11+: the clearer "cannot access local variable…" UnboundLocalError message.

Connections

Path:names & bindingscope & LEGBclosuresdecorators
  • Builds on names & binding: every scope is a namespace of bindings; this note is about which one a read reaches.
  • Used by closures: the E of LEGB, seen from inside the inner function.
  • Used by comprehensions: a comprehension has its own scope, so its loop variable doesn't leak.
  • Same mechanism as the eval loop: LOAD_FAST, LOAD_DEREF and LOAD_GLOBAL are three opcodes chosen at compile time.
  • Same idea elsewhere: JavaScript's let has a temporal dead zone, the same "declared for the whole block, unreadable before assignment" rule.

notes.title: First-Class Functions & Closures
notes.html:
References

The nonlocal statement · inspect: types and members (__closure__) · Execution model: naming and binding · Real Python: Inner functions

TL;DR

First-class = the function can leave the scope that made it. Closure = it takes the cells with it: shared, live, and read at call time.

Flow:compiler marks msg as a cell variableouter() runs and allocates the cellMAKE_FUNCTION stores it in inner.__closure__outer returns, its frame is discardedthe cell survivesinner() reads it at call time

Recall

Prompt Answer
What makes a function first-class? It's an object: assign, pass, return, store it.
Nested function vs closure? __closure__ is None vs a tuple of cells; returning doesn't make a closure.
Draw by hand: two closures, one cell outer's frame is gone; bump and get each hold __closure__ → the same cell, n = 2.
Capture by value or reference? Reference: one shared cell, read at call time.
How do you write a captured variable? nonlocal; plain assignment makes a new local.
One cell per what? Per enclosing call, so a factory isolates state and a loop doesn't.

The idea

When the enclosing function returns, where does its local go? Normally it dies with the frame:

def outer():
    msg = "hello"
    def inner(): return "standalone"
    return inner
outer().__closure__       # → None   msg was freed with the frame

inner is a first-class object that escaped, but it carried nothing. Change one thing and have it read msg:

def outer():                          # ② each call allocates a cell for msg
    msg = "hello"
    def inner(): return msg           # ① msg compiled as a free variable  ③ cell stored in __closure__
    return inner
fn = outer()                          # ④ frame discarded, cell survives
fn()                                  # ⑤ → 'hello'   the frame is gone, the value isn't
fn.__closure__[0].cell_contents       # → 'hello'
fn.__code__.co_freevars               # → ('msg',)

Something kept msg alive: a cell, a one-slot heap object that the returned function holds. It's neither dead nor copied. It's shared and live, so two closures from the same call see each other's writes:

def outer():
    n = 0
    def bump():
        nonlocal n; n += 1            # write THROUGH the cell
    def get(): return n               # read the same cell
    return bump, get
bump, get = outer(); bump(); bump()
get()                                 # → 2

The trade: functions carry live private state with no class and no boilerplate, and you pay by keeping everything in those cells alive as long as the function lives, and by reading the value at call time, not creation time.

How it works

One extra level of indirection, decided at compile time:

The rules behind ① to ⑤:

Rule What actually happens
The compiler reclassifies the name in both scopes In CPython the enclosing function lists it in co_cellvars, so its frame stores a cell instead of the value (②); the inner function lists it in co_freevars and reads it with LOAD_DEREF / STORE_DEREF instead of LOAD_FAST (①, ⑤).
Capture is by reference because nothing is copied The cell holds a pointer, the closure holds the cell, the read happens when the closure runs. That's the feature (sibling closures share state, decorators carry config) and the late-binding loop trap (LEGB).
Lifetime follows the closure, not the call An ordinary reference from __closure__ keeps the cell alive (④), so everything reachable from the captured value lives as long as the function object.
One cell per enclosing call Each call builds a fresh frame and fresh cells, so a factory gives independent state per call (see Break it).

Code

Two closures, one shared cell that nothing outside can reach:

def make_counter(start: int = 0):
    count = start                     # cellvar: inner functions reference it

    def increment(step: int = 1) -> int:
        nonlocal count                # write through the cell, not a new local
        count += step
        return count

    def value() -> int:
        return count                  # reads the SAME cell, live

    return increment, value

inc, val = make_counter(10)
inc(); inc(5)
print(val(), inc.__closure__[0].cell_contents)   # → 16 16

That privacy is real, not by convention. But if you're about to return a third closure to reset the counter, write the class.

Break it: compare the cell objects directly.

def make():
    n = 0
    def inc():
        nonlocal n; n += 1; return n
    def get(): return n
    return inc, get
a_inc, a_get = make(); b_inc, b_get = make()
a_inc(); a_inc()
print(a_get(), b_get(), a_inc.__closure__[0] is a_get.__closure__[0],
      a_inc.__closure__[0] is b_inc.__closure__[0])
# look for: siblings from ONE call share a cell; a SECOND call gets its own
# naive model predicts: all four share state, or none do

It prints 2 0 True False. Sharing is scoped to the enclosing call, which is why a factory is the reliable fix for loop capture: each call gets its own frame and cell.

Interview

30-second answer: Functions are objects, so they can be returned and stored. A nested function becomes a closure only when it references a free variable from an enclosing function. The compiler then stores that variable in a cell, and the returned function keeps the cell alive in __closure__. Capture is by reference: the cell is shared and read at call time. Writing to it needs nonlocal.

Q · Mechanism — What does CPython build when a function captures an enclosing variable? The name becomes a cellvar in the enclosing function and a freevar in the inner one. The frame stores a cell, a heap object whose cell_contents points at the value, and MAKE_FUNCTION attaches it to the inner function's __closure__. On return the frame is discarded, but refcounting keeps the cell alive. Reads use LOAD_DEREF, so they see the current value, and siblings from one call share the cell.

Q · Failure — Moving a job from a thread pool to ProcessPoolExecutor fails with a pickling error, and the old version slowly leaked memory. Both trace to closures. Explain. Closures and lambdas can't be pickled, so they can't cross a process boundary. The error often names something unrelated. The leak is lifetime: the closure captured a whole request object and was stored in a module-level registry, so the cell pinned it for the process. Tests with one call see neither. Fix: submit a top-level function (or functools.partial over one) with explicit arguments, and capture only the fields you need.

Q · Design — Design a closure-based rate-limiter factory used across a service. Where does it break versus a class? The constraint is per-caller isolation, and closures give it for free: each make_limiter(rate) call gets fresh cells for tokens and last_refill, with allow() updating them via nonlocal. It breaks when the interface grows (reset(), metrics), since cells are invisible in debuggers and logs and can't be pickled; switch to a class then. It isn't thread-safe: tokens -= 1 through a cell needs a captured Lock. Watch RSS against request volume first, which catches a factory called per request instead of per client.

Compare

Closure Class instance
State lives in shared cells (__closure__) __dict__ / __slots__
Interface one callable many named methods
Privacy genuinely unreachable by convention
Picklable if attributes are
Debuggability opaque cells named attributes

Pitfalls

  • "A closure copies the enclosing variables"
    It shares a live cell with the enclosing scope.
    ↳ Symptom: later writes in the outer function show up in the closure, which is the loop-variable trap.
  • "I can just assign to the enclosing variable"
    Assignment makes it local to the inner function.
    ↳ Symptom: count += 1 raises UnboundLocalError.
    ↳ Fix: nonlocal count.
  • "Returning a function makes it a closure"
    Only capturing a free variable does.
    ↳ Check: a nested function that uses nothing outer has __closure__ is None.
  • Not the same as a generator
    ↳ Difference: a closure keeps a few captured bindings; a generator keeps its whole suspended frame (locals, position, open blocks).
    ↳ Short: closures remember values, generators remember where they were.
  • Don't capture large or resource-holding objects casually (requests, DB handles, DataFrames).
    ↳ Why: a closure stored in a registry or callback list keeps them alive for the whole process.
    ↳ Symptom: slow memory growth with no obvious owner.
  • Don't assume closure state is thread-safe.
    ↳ Why: count += 1 through a cell is read, add, write, not atomic; threads lose updates.
    ↳ Instead: a lock, or an object built for counting.
  • 🔖 Version: nonlocal is 3.0+, so count = [0] tricks are Python 2 habits.
    ↳ 3.7+: writable cell_contents.

Connections

Path:scope & LEGBclosuresdecoratorsfunctools
  • Builds on LEGB: a closure cell is the E, seen from inside the inner function.
  • Used by decorators: the wrapper is a closure over the wrapped function and its config.
  • Contrasts with generators: a closure keeps a few variables; a generator keeps its whole running frame.
  • Contrasts with functools.partial: pre-bound arguments in an inspectable, picklable object instead of hidden cells.
  • Same idea elsewhere: JavaScript closures capture by reference too, with the same var-in-a-loop trap that let fixed.

notes.title: The Arguments Model (/, *, *args, **kwargs)
notes.html:
References

Reference: calls · 📜 PEP 570: positional-only parameters · 📜 PEP 3102: keyword-only arguments · Real Python: args and kwargs demystified

TL;DR

/ makes names private (rename-safe); * makes names required (self-documenting). In a def the stars pack; at a call site they unpack.

Flow:call f(...)positionals fill parameters left to rightextras go to *args or raisekeywords bind by nameextras go to **kwargs or raiseunfilled parameters take their defaults or raise

Recall

Prompt Answer
Full parameter order? pos_only, /, pos_or_kw, *args, kw_only, **kwargs.
What do / and * mark? Before / is positional-only; after * is keyword-only.
Stars in a def vs a call? def packs into tuple/dict; a call unpacks an iterable/mapping.

The idea

By default every parameter is positional-or-keyword, and that has a cost you don't see:

def connect(host, port): ...
connect("db", 5432); connect(host="db", port=5432)   # → both work, indistinguishable

The moment anyone writes connect(host="db"), renaming host to hostname is a breaking change. By default every parameter name is a promise you've made. Two markers take that choice back:

def connect(host, port, /, timeout=30, *, retries=3): ...
connect("db", 5432, 10, retries=5)    # → ok
connect(host="db", port=5432)         # ② → TypeError: positional-only arguments passed as keyword
connect("db", 5432, 10, 5)            # ① → TypeError: takes from 2 to 3 positional arguments but 4 were given

def connect(host, port, /, timeout=30, *, retries=3, **opts)
            └─ positional-only ┘ └ either ┘  └ keyword-only ┘ └ extra keywords → dict
               names PRIVATE      public      name IS the contract

A bare * collects nothing; it's only a marker. *args with a name collects extra positionals into a tuple. And at a call site the stars reverse meaning: connect(*args, **kw) spreads a tuple and a dict into arguments.

The trade: you give up the caller's freedom to choose, and get back rename-safe positional names and call sites that can't pass cryptic bare booleans.

How it works

Binding runs in a fixed order, and each step has its own error (messages verified on CPython 3.12 for def f(a, b, /, c=3, *, d)):

Defaults fill gaps last, and those objects were built once when def ran (the mutable-default trap). In CPython the three boundaries live on the code object as co_posonlyargcount, co_argcount and co_kwonlyargcount. Repeating a keyword in one call (c=3, c=4) never reaches binding: it's a SyntaxError.

Code

Each marker placement is an API decision:

def create_user(name, email, /, role="viewer", *, send_email=True, dry_run=False, **extra):
    #           └ positional-only ┘ └ either ┘   └──── keyword-only ────┘   └ overflow ┘
    return {"name": name, "email": email, "role": role,
            "send_email": send_email, "dry_run": dry_run, **extra}

create_user("Raje", "r@x.io", send_email=False)   # flags self-document
# create_user("Raje", "r@x.io", False, True)      # TypeError, and unreadable anyway
# create_user(name="Raje", email="r@x.io")        # TypeError: names stay rename-safe
create_user("Raje", "r@x.io", **{"role": "admin"})   # unpack at the call site

name/email are obvious in context, so their names shouldn't become a promise; that's also why len, dict.get and str.replace are positional-only. The booleans are keyword-only because positional flags are unreadable and break silently if reordered.

Interview

30-second answer: In a signature, *args collects extra positionals into a tuple and **kwargs collects extra keywords into a dict. At a call site the same stars unpack an iterable or mapping into arguments. A bare * is a marker: everything after it is keyword-only. / makes everything before it positional-only. They're API tools: / keeps names private, * forces readable call sites.

Q · Mechanism — Why deliberately make a parameter positional-only or keyword-only in a production API? Positional-only decouples names from the contract: nobody can write f(x=…), so you can rename in a patch release. It also lets a parameter named self or key coexist with the same key passed through **kwargs. Keyword-only forces the caller to name the argument, killing the create_user("admin", True, False) bug where nobody can tell what the booleans mean. Together: hide names you might rename, force clarity on options.

Compare

Marker Caller must use Name public?
a (default) position or keyword frozen once anyone names it
a, / position only private, rename freely
*, a keyword only the name is the contract
*args / **kwargs — collectors: tuple / dict
bare * — marker, collects nothing

Pitfalls

  • "* and ** mean the same in a def and a call"
    Opposite directions: def packs, a call unpacks.
    ↳ Symptom: mixing them up causes "got multiple values for argument" errors.
  • "A bare * accepts extra positionals"
    It collects nothing.
    ↳ What it does: forces every parameter after it to be keyword-only, so callers can't rely on order for flags like verbose.
  • Not the same as the shared-default trap
    ↳ Difference: this note is how values reach parameters at call time; that one is when defaults were created (def-time).
    ↳ Why it matters: confusing them leads to the wrong fix.
  • Don't absorb known options into a sprawling **kwargs.
    ↳ Why: no completion, no type checking, useless help(), and typos are silently accepted.
    ↳ Instead: explicit parameters, or TypedDict + Unpack for a fixed forwarded set.
  • Don't put a required parameter after *args expecting it positional.
    ↳ Why: everything after *args is keyword-only.
    ↳ Symptom: f(1, 2, 3) puts all three in args, then fails for the missing keyword.
  • 🔖 Version: / positional-only 3.8+ (PEP 570); * keyword-only 3.0+ (PEP 3102).
    ↳ Typing: ParamSpec 3.10+, TypeVarTuple/Unpack 3.11+.

Connections

Path:closuresarguments modeldecoratorsfunctools.partial
  • Builds on names & binding: parameters are ordinary bindings made at call time.
  • Builds on mutable defaults: the last step reuses objects built at def time.
  • Used by decorators: *args, **kwargs is how a wrapper passes any call through unchanged.
  • Used by functools.partial: pre-binds some arguments, so the same binding rules apply later.
  • Same idea elsewhere: Kotlin and Swift named arguments; Swift's argument labels make the name part of the contract, like keyword-only here.

notes.title: Decorators
notes.html:
References

Function definitions (decorator grammar) · functools.wraps · 📜 PEP 614: relaxed decorator grammar · Real Python: Primer on decorators

TL;DR

@deco is f = deco(f): once, at definition time, rebinding the name. Application is bottom-up; execution is top-down; @deco(arg) adds a third layer.

Flow:@a over @b over def fdef builds f0b(f0) returns wba(wb) returns wathe name f is bound to wa, oncelater f(x) enters wa, then wb, then f0, and unwinds the other way

Recall

Prompt Answer
What does @deco desugar to? f = deco(f), run once right after def builds the function.
What does functools.wraps preserve? __name__, __qualname__, __doc__, __module__, __dict__; sets __wrapped__.
Stacking order? @a over @b is a(b(f)): bottom-up application, top-down execution.
@deco(arg): how many layers? Three: factory → decorator → wrapper. It's deco(arg)(f).
Draw by hand: @a over @b, def time and call time def: b(f0) → wb, a(wb) → wa. call: wa → wb → f0, unwinding through b then a.
Sync decorator on async def? Returns the coroutine unawaited; the body never runs, nothing raises.

The idea

What is @ actually shorthand for? You already have everything it does. def binds a name, and nothing stops you rebinding it to something built from the original:

def logged(func):
    def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
        print(f"calling {func.__name__}")
        return func(*args, **kwargs)
    return wrapper

def greet(name): return f"hello {name}"
greet = logged(greet)
greet("Raje")          # → calling greet · 'hello Raje'

No call site changed; they still reach whatever greet names, which is now a closure holding the original. @logged above the def is exactly that assignment, moved to where a reader sees it first. It runs once, and its return value becomes the function, so @deco returning 42 makes f an integer.

The useful version broke something, though:

greet.__name__, greet.__doc__    # → ('wrapper', None)

The name points at a different object with its own metadata, so tracebacks, help(), inspect.signature and anything keyed on __name__ (routers, test collectors) see wrapper. Adding @functools.wraps(func) above def wrapper copies the original's identity across and sets __wrapped__.

The trade: cross-cutting behaviour moves out of every function body into one declaration above the signature, and you pay by replacing the function object, so you must carry its identity across by hand.

How it works

Two decorators, two timelines: definition time, then call time (order verified on CPython 3.12):

The rules around that timeline:

Rule What actually happens
Stacking is nesting f = a(b(f)): applied bottom-up at def time, executed top-down at call time (the diagram). Giving only one half is the classic half-learned answer.
Arguments make a factory @retry(max_attempts=3) is f = retry(max_attempts=3)(f): the retry(3) call runs first and must return a decorator, so it's three nested functions (factory, decorator, wrapper).
The wrapper's signature makes it reusable (*args, **kwargs) forwards everything (arguments model); a hard-coded signature fits one function, and a missing return before func(...) turns every result into None.
Decorators can't see coroutine-ness A sync wrapper around an async def returns the coroutine unawaited. Async layers need async def wrapper with await func(...), or a branch on inspect.iscoroutinefunction(func) at decoration time.

Code

A production retry decorator, with the three details that pass review:

import functools, time

def retry(max_attempts: int = 3, backoff: float = 0.1):   # factory: captures config
    def decorator(func):                                  # the actual decorator
        @functools.wraps(func)                            # carry identity across
        def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
            for attempt in range(1, max_attempts + 1):
                try:
                    return func(*args, **kwargs)          # MUST return, or you get None
                except ConnectionError:                   # narrow: don't retry bugs
                    if attempt == max_attempts:
                        raise
                    time.sleep(backoff * 2 ** (attempt - 1))
        return wrapper
    return decorator

@retry(max_attempts=3)
def fetch(url: str) -> str:
    """Fetch a URL."""
    return "ok"

print(fetch.__name__, fetch.__wrapped__)   # → fetch <function fetch ...>

Break it: put a print in the decorator body itself.

def noisy(func):
    print(f"DECORATING {func.__name__}")
    def wrapper(*a, **kw):
        print("  wrapper running"); return func(*a, **kw)
    return wrapper
@noisy
def f(): return 1
print("--- def finished, nothing called ---")
f(); f(); print(f.__name__)
# look for: DECORATING prints once, BEFORE the marker; wrapper prints per call
# naive model predicts: DECORATING on every call, and __name__ == 'f'

You get DECORATING f, the marker, wrapper running twice, then wrapper. Decoration is an import-time cost paid once, and the name is genuinely bound to a new object; adding wraps flips the last line to f.

Interview

30-second answer: @deco above a def is f = deco(f), run once at definition time. The decorator returns a replacement, usually a closure wrapping the original, and the name is rebound to it. Stacked decorators apply bottom-up and execute top-down. With arguments it's a three-layer factory. Always use functools.wraps in the wrapper, or the function reports itself as wrapper everywhere.

Q · Mechanism — What does Python do when it evaluates @my_decorator above a def, and in what order for stacked decorators? It builds the function object, calls my_decorator(func), and binds the return value to the name. For module functions that's import time; afterwards only the wrapper runs per call. For @a over @b, it's a(b(f)): b wraps the raw function first, but a call enters a's wrapper first and unwinds back through b. Layers are applied from the inside out; calls knock on the outermost door first.

Q · Failure — After adding a shared @timed decorator to async FastAPI handlers, some endpoints return a coroutine object and their side effects stop happening. No errors. Diagnose. @timed has a sync wrapper. It calls the async def, gets a coroutine, and returns it without awaiting, so the handler body never runs. Nothing raises at decoration time, and sync-only tests pass. A sibling risk is a missing return func(...), which silently returns None. Fix: an async def wrapper that awaits, or branch on inspect.iscoroutinefunction at decoration time. Add a contract test asserting decorated and undecorated handlers return the same value.

Q · Design — Design a stackable decorator layer for auth, rate limiting, retries and metrics on endpoint handlers. Where does it break? Order is the binding constraint because the stack is a pipeline. Metrics outermost, to time retries and rejections; auth next, rejecting before work; then rate limiting; retries innermost, so a retry doesn't re-auth or count as three requests. Each layer is a wraps-preserving (*args, **kwargs) wrapper; configurable ones are factories. It breaks on runtime flexibility: decorators bind at def-time to one function, so per-deployment policy, kill switches or third-party routes need ASGI middleware or Depends. Watch handlers returning unexpected None first.

Compare

Function decorator Class decorator (__call__)
State closure cells instance attributes
Best for simple wrap-and-forward rich, introspectable state (counts, registries)
Identity @functools.wraps(func) functools.update_wrapper(self, func)
On methods works naturally needs __get__ to bind self

Pitfalls

  • "A decorator runs on every call"
    The decorator runs once, at def-time; only its wrapper runs per call.
    ↳ So: setup in the decorator body is paid once, usually at import (see Break it).
  • "@deco and @deco(arg) are the same shape"
    @deco(arg) is a factory: three layers, deco(arg)(f).
    ↳ Symptom: two layers plus an argument gives a TypeError or a wrapper that never wraps.
  • "A decorator must return a function"
    It can return anything, and that becomes the name's value.
    ↳ Examples: property, staticmethod, classmethod return descriptors; a decorator returning None turns your function into None.
  • Not the same as a closure
    ↳ Difference: a decorator is the pattern (replace and rebind at def-time); a closure is the usual mechanism.
    ↳ Example: __call__ classes and lru_cache are decorators with no closure.
  • Don't put @cache / @lru_cache on an instance method.
    ↳ Why: the key includes self, so every instance stays alive for the life of the process.
    ↳ Instead: cached_property or a per-instance cache (see functools-toolkit).
  • Don't use decorators for app-wide or runtime-configurable policy.
    ↳ Why: they bind once, at def-time, to one function.
    ↳ Instead: middleware or dependency injection for per-deployment rules, kill switches, third-party routes.
  • 🔖 Version: PEP 614 (3.9+) allows any expression after @.
    ↳ Also: functools.cache 3.9+, ParamSpec for typed decorators 3.10+.

Connections

Path:closuresdecoratorsfunctoolsdescriptors
  • Builds on closures: the wrapper is a closure over the original function.
  • Builds on the arguments model: *args, **kwargs is the universal pass-through.
  • Used by functools: wraps, lru_cache and cached_property are all applied as decorators.
  • Used by descriptors: @property builds a descriptor; class decorators are the lighter alternative to a metaclass.
  • Same idea elsewhere: Java and TypeScript annotations look similar but are metadata; a Python decorator actually replaces the object.

notes.title: The functools Toolkit (lru_cache, partial, singledispatch, cached_property, reduce)
notes.html:
References

functools — higher-order functions · functools.cached_property · Real Python: Caching with lru_cache

TL;DR

Every functools tool gives a hand-rolled pattern a named owner and a lifetime. lru_cache lives on the function (process lifetime); cached_property lives on the instance.

Flow:f(args)key built from all args (must be hashable)hit: stored result, body skippedmiss: run body, storepast maxsize: evict least recently used

Recall

Prompt Answer
The two lru_cache traps? Process-lifetime memory (pins self on methods); arguments must be hashable.
partial vs a lambda? partial exposes .func/.args/.keywords and pickles over top-level functions.
cached_property vs lru_cache on a method? Stored in the instance __dict__, so it dies with the instance.

The idea

Each tool replaces a hand-rolled pattern with a quiet defect: a module-level _memo = {} that grows forever, an unpicklable, opaque lambda, an isinstance chain edited centrally for every new type:

@functools.lru_cache(maxsize=128)
def slow(n): return n ** 2
slow(4); slow(4); slow.cache_info()   # → CacheInfo(hits=1, misses=1, maxsize=128, currsize=1)
double = functools.partial(operator.mul, 2)
double.func, double.args              # → (<built-in function mul>, (2,))
slow([1, 2])                          # → TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'

The last line is the part people miss. The cache is a dict keyed on the arguments, so they must be hashable, and it lives on the function object, so its lifetime is the process's. maxsize bounds entry count, not bytes: 128 entries could be ints or DataFrames. On a method it's worse, because self is part of every key:

The trade: you get bounded, inspectable, extensible versions of hand-rolled patterns, and in exchange a cache becomes process-lifetime shared state living somewhere you didn't put it.

How it works

Tool What actually happens
lru_cache Follows the Flow line. On an instance method the key includes self and the table holds a strong reference to it (see the picture).
cached_property A non-data descriptor: the first access computes the value and writes it into the instance's __dict__ under the same name. An instance dict shadows a non-data descriptor, so later reads never reach it.
singledispatch Dispatches on the first argument's type; @fn.register adds handlers from any module, so new types extend it without editing a central if/elif.

Code

The comments carry the decisions:

import functools, operator

@functools.lru_cache(maxsize=1024)          # ALWAYS bound it; watch cache_info()
def resolve_tenant(tenant_id: str) -> dict: # hashable args, deterministic, no side effects
    return {"id": tenant_id}

double = functools.partial(operator.mul, 2) # picklable: safe for ProcessPoolExecutor

@functools.singledispatch                   # dispatches on the FIRST arg's type
def render(value) -> str:
    return str(value)

@render.register                            # new types register from anywhere
def _(value: list) -> str:
    return ", ".join(render(v) for v in value)

class Dataset:
    def __init__(self, rows): self.rows = rows
    @functools.cached_property              # per-instance memo, dies with the instance;
    def stats(self) -> dict:                # @lru_cache here would pin every Dataset
        return {"n": len(self.rows)}

Interview

30-second answer: lru_cache memoises by arguments into a table on the function object, so bound it with maxsize and keep arguments hashable. cached_property memoises a zero-argument property on the instance itself. partial pre-binds arguments in an inspectable, picklable object, unlike a lambda. singledispatch gives open, type-based overloading on the first argument. reduce rarely beats sum, math.prod or a loop.

Q · Mechanism — Why does @lru_cache on an instance method leak memory, and what do you use instead? The table lives on the function object, alive for the process, and every key holds self strongly (the picture), so RSS tracks cumulative instances rather than live ones. maxsize caps the damage but not the cause, and functools.cache is unbounded. Use cached_property for zero-arg per-instance values, an explicit dict on the instance for parameterised ones, or a module-level function keyed on immutable fields for a genuinely shared cache.

Compare

Tool State lives Key trap
lru_cache / cache on the function, process lifetime unbounded without maxsize; hashable args; pins self
cached_property instance __dict__ first compute can race across threads
partial the partial object caller can override pre-bound keywords
singledispatch registry on the function first argument only
reduce — usually less readable than a built-in

Pitfalls

  • "lru_cache is a free speedup for anything"
    It's process-lifetime shared state.
    ↳ Why: it grows to maxsize (forever with @cache), holds strong refs to every argument and result, and is shared by all callers and tests.
    ↳ Treat it as: a cache: bounded, deterministic, invalidated deliberately.
  • Not the same as cached_property
    ↳ Difference: lru_cache stores in one global table and keeps self alive on methods; cached_property stores on the instance and is freed with it.
  • Don't cache non-deterministic or side-effecting calls (clock, DB, network, mutation).
    ↳ Why: the cache returns stale results confidently; nothing signals it, so stale is worse than slow.
  • Don't cache functions that take lists, dicts or sets.
    ↳ Why: arguments must be hashable: TypeError, and hashing a mutable "fix" risks keys that change under the cache.
    ↳ Instead: convert to a tuple or frozenset, or don't cache.
  • Don't forget cache_clear() in tests.
    ↳ Symptom: results leak between tests, so tests pass alone and fail together.
    ↳ Fix: clear in a fixture.
  • 🔖 Version: cache 3.9+; cached_property and bare @lru_cache 3.8+; union types in singledispatch 3.11+.
    ↳ 3.12: cached_property dropped its lock, so concurrent first access can compute twice.

Connections

Path:decoratorsfunctoolsdescriptors
  • Builds on decorators: every tool here is applied as one.
  • Builds on the eq/hash contract: cache keys are dict keys, so arguments must be hashable.
  • Same mechanism as descriptors: cached_property works because an instance dict shadows a non-data descriptor.
  • Used by multiprocessing: partial of a top-level function pickles; a lambda doesn't.
  • Breaks when combined with reference counting: a cache's strong references keep objects alive (the picture).
